transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. Can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me?

Well, I guess... what brings me in is that I just can’t keep my words in a straight line anymore, you know? It's like, I'll be talking to someone, maybe one of the nurses at work—I'm a psychiatric aide, by the way, mostly overnight shifts, which are supposed to be quiet but never really are—and I'll start trying to tell them about something simple that happened on the shift, like getting a patient a blanket. But then, before I even realize it, my brain just sort of... jumps tracks. I'll go from talking about the overnight shift to suddenly talking about soccer, because maybe the blanket was blue and that reminds me of a soccer jersey I saw once, and then from soccer I'm talking about paint colors, like the exact shade of eggshell white on the walls in the day room, and then somehow I'm rambling about patient charts and how the tabs are color-coded. And I can see it on their faces. I can see everyone getting lost, like their eyes just glaze over or they get this confused, almost pitying look, and I know I'm not making sense, but I can't stop the words from spilling out in this huge, messy pile. It's just so frustrating because I know what I want to say when I start, but it's like the bridge between my brain and my mouth is completely broken, and I end up taking these massive detours that don't make sense to anyone but me, and honestly, half the time they don't even make sense to me by the time I'm done talking. It's just... it's exhausting, really, having to constantly backtrack and apologize because I can't just tell a simple story from point A to point B anymore without hitting every other letter of the alphabet along the way.
Over this same period, have you noticed your mood feeling unusually elevated, euphoric, or irritable, along with having much more energy than usual and needing very little sleep?

No, no, definitely not that. I mean, elevated? Euphoric? God, I wish. No, it’s... it’s actually the complete opposite. I don’t have energy. I have no energy at all. It’s like someone pulled the plug on me, you know? Like, I’ll be at work, walking down the hall, and it literally feels like I’m dragging heavy chains behind me. Every step is just so much effort. And sleep? I wish I needed little sleep. I feel like I could sleep for a thousand years and still wake up tired. When I get home from a shift, I just collapse into bed, and even then, I don't want to get up. I just lie there, staring at the ceiling, feeling this heavy, dark weight pressing down on my chest. It’s not just being tired from the overnight shift, it’s this deep, bone-crushing exhaustion where even lifting my arm to turn off the alarm clock feels like running a marathon. And irritable? Well, maybe a little, but mostly just because I’m so drained and everything feels so pointless and gray. There’s no euphoria, no high, no sudden bursts of energy where I want to clean my apartment or start a new project. It’s just... flat. Everything is just flat and heavy and dark, all the time. I haven't felt anything close to euphoric in... I don't even know how long. It's just a constant struggle to keep my eyes open and put one foot in front of the other.
Have you ever noticed this jumbled, disorganized way of speaking happening even during times when you weren't feeling depressed or low in energy?

Yeah, actually, I have... and it's not just the talking thing, either. I mean, yes, the words getting all tangled up happens even when I'm not feeling like I'm dragging those chains around. But there's this other thing, too. Like, there was this one stretch—I don't know, maybe a few weeks, maybe a month ago?—where the heavy, dark feeling actually lifted for a bit. I wasn't feeling that crushing exhaustion, and I could actually get out of bed without feeling like I was lifting a boulder off my chest. I thought maybe I was getting better, you know? But even then... even when the depression wasn't there, I still couldn't shake this... this feeling at work. 

I kept thinking—no, I *knew*—that the cameras in the hallways, the ones they say are just for patient safety, were actually focused specifically on me. I'd walk past the nursing station, and I could feel the lens tracking my movements. And it wasn't just the cameras. I was convinced the supervisors were constantly monitoring me, like they had some secret channel where they were analyzing everything I did, every time I handed out a towel or checked a room. I was so guarded, so careful about every single step I took, because I felt like any little mistake was being recorded and scrutinized. I wouldn't even look the charge nurse in the eye because I thought she was in on it, reporting back to whoever was watching the feeds. So, even when I wasn't depressed, my brain was still doing all this... this extra stuff, making me paranoid and messing up how I talked to people because I was so focused on trying not to give anything away to the cameras. It's like, even when one thing stops, the other stuff just keeps going.

Looking back over the whole time you've been dealing with this—how much of that total time would you say you were experiencing the depressed, low-energy mood, compared to the time you had the paranoid thoughts or jumbled speech without feeling depressed at all?

Well, if I'm really looking back at all of it... the whole timeline, I mean... it's mostly been the depression. That heavy, empty feeling, the one where I just don't care about anything and have no energy at all? That's been there for almost the entire time this has been going on. It's like this thick, gray fog that just settled over my life and refuses to lift, you know? Even when the other stuff—the feeling that the cameras were watching me, or when my words would get all tangled up into that messy pile I was talking about earlier—even when those things would kind of quiet down or fade into the background for a little while, that crushing exhaustion and just total lack of interest in anything was still there. 

I mean, I'd go to work, and maybe I wasn't quite as panicked about the supervisors watching my every move on the monitors, but I still felt like I was dragging those heavy chains down the hallway. I still didn't want to be there. I didn't want to talk to the patients, I didn't want to talk to the nurses, I didn't even want to go home and watch TV or do anything I used to like. I just wanted to sleep, but even sleep didn't help. So, yeah, if I had to measure it out, the depressed mood, that total emptiness... that's been the main thing, the constant thing, taking up the vast majority of this whole period. The paranoid thoughts and the jumbled speech, they definitely happen on their own sometimes, like I said, but they're more like... like spikes or waves on top of this massive, deep ocean of just feeling completely drained and hopeless. It's almost always the depression that's running the show, even when the other stuff decides to take a break.

During that stretch when your mood lifted and you weren't feeling depressed, but you still had the paranoid thoughts about the cameras and the jumbled speech—about how many days or weeks did that period last?

Well, if I'm trying to pin down exactly how long that specific stretch lasted... the time when the heavy, gray fog kind of lifted but the cameras were still, you know, tracking me... I'd say it was probably a few weeks. Yeah, a few weeks, maybe a little more, but definitely in that ballpark. I remember it so clearly because it was just such a weird contrast. Like, I was waking up and I didn't have that immediate, crushing thought of, "Oh god, I have to exist today." I could actually get out of bed without feeling like I was peeling myself off the mattress, and when I walked into the hospital for my shift, my legs didn't feel like they were made of lead. I wasn't exhausted in that bone-deep way. 

But even though I had the energy to do my job, to hand out the linens and check the rooms and do all the orderly stuff, my mind was just completely hijacked by the cameras. It was during those few weeks that I was so hyper-aware of every little red light blinking on the security domes in the ceiling. I'd be walking down the corridor, feeling physically okay, not depressed, but my heart would be racing because I just knew, I absolutely knew, that the supervisors were sitting in their office, zoomed in on me. I was so guarded. I mean, I was acting like a secret agent or something just trying to do my job. I'd calculate exactly how to turn the corner so I wouldn't look suspicious, and I'd rehearse what I was going to say to the nurses so I wouldn't sound guilty of... whatever it was I thought they were looking for. And that's when my words would get all tangled up, too, because I was trying so hard to control everything. So, yeah, I wasn't in that deep, depressed place for those few weeks, but I was still completely wrapped up in the belief that I was being monitored every single second I was on the clock. It was exhausting in a completely different way, honestly.
